title: Sleep and Recovery
subtitle: Make room for rest so movement fits your real life.

blocks.text: A fitness app may send a cheerful reminder to exercise at the exact moment you finally sit down. Its calendar has never worked a late shift or settled a child after midnight. Rest deserves space in your plan, even when the reminder has excellent graphics.
What you will learn

items.title: Tell sleep opportunity apart from time actually asleep
Build a wind-down routine around your responsibilities
Choose easier movement or rest when needed
Use a private seven-day review to choose one change

blocks.text: Recovery means giving yourself time and support to feel ready after activity and everyday demands. Sleep is part of recovery, alongside breaks and manageable movement. A demanding workday counts when you decide how much extra activity fits.

Time set aside for sleep is your sleep opportunity. Time actually asleep can be shorter because settling down and waking during the night use some of that space. Eight hours between getting into bed and getting up does not prove eight hours of sleep.
CSEP recommends regular good-quality sleep: generally 7–9 hours for adults aged 18–64 and 7–8 hours for adults aged 65 and older. Your work or caregiving schedule may need its own pattern.

This lesson offers general learning, not insomnia treatment or a medical plan. Ask a clinician about persistent sleep trouble, loud snoring with breathing pauses, or daytime sleepiness that affects daily tasks. Never drive while drowsy.
Room to recover
blocks.detail: Recognizing the rest you need helps you choose activity that fits the day you actually have.

blocks.text: Start with the responsibilities that shape your sleep window. A shift worker may need daytime sleep, while a caregiver may have broken nights. Look for a routine you can repeat within similar kinds of days, rather than copying someone else’s bedtime.

Prepare a quiet, dark space at a comfortable temperature. Choose one change you can afford, such as closing a blind or asking others to keep noise down. You do not need to replace your mattress before trying a small improvement.
Protect a window, not a score. Write down when sleep could fit before buying a tracker; a device cannot create time that work and caregiving have already used.

Give your final tasks a stopping point before sleep. For example, put tomorrow’s lunch in the fridge, leave a note for an unfinished chore, and move work messages out of reach. Choose a quiet activity that does not become another job to finish.

Caffeine can keep you alert when you want to sleep, and alcohol can disrupt sleep even if it makes you feel sleepy at first. Notice their timing relative to your sleep window. Ask a pharmacist or clinician about medicine concerns rather than changing prescribed treatment yourself.

items.title: “Alcohol is a reliable sleep aid.”
items.text: Feeling sleepy after drinking does not mean sleep will be restful; alcohol can cause more waking.

blocks.text: Recovery also belongs in your movement plan. After a demanding day, choose a shorter familiar activity, an easier version, or rest instead of adding another hard session. Ordinary meals and access to water can be part of that plan, without turning recovery into a shopping list of supplements. For example, pack your usual sandwich and fruit for after a workday walk, and bring water rather than leaving it at home.
Make the easier option specific. “Walk gently for five minutes if comfortable” is a clearer backup than “do something”; taking a rest day is also a valid choice.

sections.title: Fictional learning story: The curtain note

blocks.text: The curtain note
paragraphs: Mara worked rotating shifts at a Saskatoon food plant. She wanted enough energy to join her sister’s Saturday walks without spending the afternoon on the sofa. Her kitchen calendar had walking dates, but no space marked for rest.

After three late shifts, Mara slept through their meeting time. Her sister’s message was kind, yet Mara worried their weekly time together would disappear. She decided to look at her week before agreeing to another early start.

For seven days, she privately noted the sleep window she had planned and roughly how rested she felt after waking. The gaps were clear: laundry and grocery trips were filling the hours she meant to protect. Adding a longer walk would not solve those gaps.

Mara could keep the early Saturday meeting or ask for a later one. She called her sister, moved the walk to the afternoon, and asked her housemate to leave laundry until she woke. She also chose a ten-minute easy walk instead of her usual longer route after late shifts.

The first protected morning still went badly because sunlight spilled past the bedroom curtain. Her housemate found the note asking for quiet and pointed out that the curtain had slipped off one hook. Fixing it took two minutes, which was far easier than the new blackout curtains Mara had started pricing.

The next week was mixed, with one unexpected shift change. Mara kept two planned sleep windows and joined the shorter Saturday walk; she did not claim that every tired day was gone. Beside the next walking date, she wrote “rest window” and drew a tiny curtain hook.

blocks.text: Make the week workable
blocks.detail: One practical change to your schedule or space can make rest easier to protect without rebuilding your whole life.

blocks.text: Ask for a defined change. A request such as “Could laundry wait until I wake on Tuesday?” gives someone a clear way to help.

Choose one sleep window that fits tomorrow’s duties, then prepare for it. Treat the plan below as an adjustable learning example, not an individual prescription. It does not ask you to shorten sleep or force yourself to sleep on command.
Adjustable 15-minute wind-down example

items.title: Minutes 0–5: finish one needed preparation, such as setting out work clothes
Minutes 5–8: lower room light and put non-urgent messages aside
Minutes 8–15: read something quiet or listen to gentle music
Total: 5 + 3 + 7 = 15 minutes before your planned sleep window

blocks.text: If fifteen minutes does not fit, try five minutes for one helpful step. Keep essential caregiving or emergency contact available. The routine is an invitation to settle, not a test you fail if you remain awake.
A shorter wind-down is an option for a busy day. It is not a reason to shorten the sleep opportunity you were trying to protect.
Observe for seven days

On days 1–3, privately note your planned sleep window, a rough sleep estimate if useful, and how ready you feel for ordinary tasks. On days 4–6, try one change, such as reducing room light. On day 7, review what helped and what still needs support; repeat the week if useful.

For movement, decide before starting whether today calls for a familiar session, an easier option, or rest. Low energy differs from pain or an injury, which you should not push through. Stop with new pain, dizziness, chest discomfort, or unusual breathlessness, and seek appropriate care.
Change one thing at a time. Keeping the rest of your plan steady makes it easier to notice whether the change is useful.

items.title: “A missed workout must be added to tomorrow.”
items.text: Doubling the next session can crowd out recovery; return to a manageable plan instead.

blocks.text: Insider tip: Keep a simple indoor option for icy paths, extreme cold, or smoky summer air. Checking local conditions before an outdoor session can save the effort of getting ready for an unsuitable route.
Quick Check

items.title: Does eight hours in bed prove eight hours asleep?
items.text: Time awake can use part of the sleep opportunity.

items.title: What can you choose after a demanding shift?
items.detail: An easier familiar activity or rest can fit the day.

items.title: Should you drive when you feel drowsy?

blocks.text: Knowledge Check

items.title: Lee has eight hours available for sleep but is awake for part of it. Which is accurate? A. Lee certainly slept eight hours. · B. Sleep opportunity and actual sleep can differ. · C. Lee must exercise longer.
items.text: Time available includes time awake, so it cannot confirm the amount slept.

items.title: Sam finishes a tiring shift before a planned walk. What fits this lesson? A. Double the walking time. · B. Ignore new pain. · C. Choose an easier version or rest.
items.text: Daily demands matter when choosing activity; pain should not be pushed through.

items.title: Jo hears that their partner snores loudly and has breathing pauses. What should Jo suggest? A. Get clinician advice. · B. Diagnose the cause from a tracker. · C. Try alcohol before sleep.
items.text: Breathing pauses need professional advice, and this course cannot identify the cause.

items.title: Write one sleep-support step and a review time that could fit a changing schedule.
items.text: After each late shift, I will close the blind before settling. I will review whether this was workable after seven days.

blocks.text: Protect an achievable sleep opportunity, use a simple routine, and let your movement plan include easier days and rest.
Write your own small recovery plan in these three fields. Keep detailed sleep observations and private health information in your own notes.
Chapter completion
To finish, write when you will review your plan and one person or service you could ask for practical help. Check that your plan names a step you can take, rather than a result you must achieve.

items.title: Sleep opportunity
items.text: Time you have made available for sleep.

items.title: Actual sleep
items.text: Time spent asleep within that opportunity.

items.title: Wind-down
items.text: A short routine to help you settle before sleep.

items.title: Recovery
items.text: Time and support after activity or daily demands.

items.title: Easier day
items.text: A day with less demanding movement.

items.title: Drowsy
items.text: Sleepy enough that staying alert is difficult.
